issues_found: Source published 2018-07-13 — approximately 7.5 years before TODAY (2026-04-13), well beyond the 90-day threshold. However, this is an official Federal Reserve Monetary Policy Report submitted to Congress under the Federal Reserve Act, which carries clear archival value as a historical policy document.

Source body is truncated; only Part 1 (Recent Economic and Financial Developments) is verifiable. Parts 2 (Monetary Policy) and 3 (Summary of Economic Projections) are not accessible, so the record's claims are necessarily limited to labor market data. The record appropriately acknowledges this limitation.
source_type in the source block is listed as 'research_paper' but should more precisely be 'monetary_policy_report' to match the event_type taxonomy. Minor inconsistency.

market_structure_context is blank. While understandable for a historical labor market document, even a brief note on the rate cycle context (Fed was in a hiking cycle, raised rates four times in 2018) would add value. This is a minor omission rather than a factual error.

corrected_fields.market_structure_context: As of mid-2018, the Federal Reserve was in an active rate-hiking cycle, having raised the federal funds rate twice already in 2018 (March and June) to a target range of 1.75–2.00%. The labor market tightness documented in this report — unemployment below all FOMC participants' longer-run estimates — was a key input into the Fed's justification for continued gradual rate increases. The Fed raised rates two additional times in 2018 (September and December).
